findings.finding: The seam catches the base class `rebar.llm.errors.LLMError`, but the diagnosed failure is `LLMUnavailableError`. Any other LLMError subclass would be counted as an 'unavailable run' and reported as 'verifier behavior was not measured', which masks genuine model or verifier regressions. findings.finding: The Approach assumes every `rebar.llm.errors.LLMError` that `runner.run` raises is a provider outage. It catches the whole base class, records it in `provider_errors`, and reports any such run as 'verifier behavior was not measured'. errors.py contradicts this: several `LLMError` subclasses are documented as NOT provider failures. `StructuredOutputError`/`UnretryableOutputError` mean the verifier's own turn failed the `verification` contract (a model output defect, which verify_findings itself logs at ERROR as a contract break). `LLMBudgetExhaustedError` and `RunawayToolLoopError` mean rebar stopped the agent's own runaway loop. `LLMInputRejectedError` is documented as 'must never be mistaken for an outage'. Under the plan as written, a real verifier regression that shows up as a shape failure or a runaway tool loop (possible in the agentic modes) would be reported as a provider outage. That is the reverse of the misreport the plan sets out to fix.

findings.finding: The plan does not say where the per-run 'unavailable' decision is made. It specifies a per-test `provider_errors` list and says a run counts as unavailable when 'the seam recorded an error and no verification came back'. But in two modules `run_chunk` is a closure rebuilt inside `_verify_once` on every run, and nothing in the plan says how a run knows whether *it* recorded an error, for example by comparing len(provider_errors) before and after the run, or by threading the list into `_verify_once`. 'No verification came back' is also undefined for multi-finding fixtures: none of the indices, or any one missing?
findings.location: Approach — "appends ... to a per-test `provider_errors` list ... Each run in which the seam recorded an error and no verification came back counts as an unavailable run"
scenarios: An implementer checks `provider_errors` being non-empty after the loop instead of per run, so one transient error in run 1 marks later runs as unavailable as well.
The predicate is implemented differently in the three inlined modules, so the same outage is counted differently in different tests.
